chunk_findings.detail: The new default `cfg=Config()` bypasses the repository’s config layers. `pr_body` advertises “the layered `[flow].pr_body_template`”, but when called without `cfg` — including by code using the old `pr_body(st, it, on=...)` signature — it constructs a fresh default `Config` instead of loading shipped/company/project/user layers from `repo`. For example, with a project config `.ddflow/config.toml` setting `[flow].pr_body_template = "templates/pr_body.md"`, a call such as `pr_body(st, it, on=None, repo=repo)` will ignore that knob and render the default template, violating the required layer order and user precedence [D-config-layer-order], [D-user-highest-precedence-2026-11-06]. chunk_findings.detail: `_gates` drops any gate whose `outcome` is empty or `None` (`if not rec.outcome: continue`). Markdown table cells need backslashes escaped before pipes; otherwise a literal backslash before a pipe becomes a literal backslash and leaves the pipe as a cell delimiter. When rendered into a GFM table row, the two backslashes are consumed as an escaped backslash, so the following pipe is unescaped and splits the row, reintroducing the previous row-splitting failure for notes that already contain escaped pipes.

chunk_findings.detail: The new default `cfg=Config()` bypasses the repository’s config layers. `pr_body` advertises “the layered `[flow].pr_body_template`”, but when called without `cfg` — including by code using the old `pr_body(st, it, on=...)` signature — it constructs a fresh default `Config` instead of loading shipped/company/project/user layers from `repo`. The fallback should require `cfg` or load config from `repo` rather than silently substituting an unlayered `Config()`.

`test_the_config_path_beats_the_project_template` writes the configured template path into a TOML basic string with `f'

chunk_findings.detail:
The new assertion only inspects the first line that starts with `| standards` and checks that it has five `|` characters and does not contain `next line`. If the renderer escapes the pipe but leaves the newline unhandled, the generated body can be:

next line |
```

The first line starts with `| standards`, contains five pipes (including the escaped one), and does not contain `next line`, so the test passes even though the Markdown table row is split across two lines and the second line is not a valid continuation. chunk_findings.detail: The change introduces `CELL_MAX = 200` as a hard-coded module constant and uses it to bound rendered `gate`, `outcome`, and `note` cells. The appended TOML then contains invalid escape sequences such as `\p` or `\U`, so `Config.load(repo)` inside `_body` can fail with a TOML parse error before the custom template is ever rendered.

chunk_findings.detail: Gate notes are interpolated raw into a markdown table cell. Given a gate whose note is `failed | see log\nnext line`, the row splits into extra columns and a second line, so a reader (or a later check that looks for `| gate | outcome`) no longer sees that gate’s outcome on one row. Notes come from review reasons, which routinely contain `|` and newlines.

chunk_findings.detail: The new `_cell` escapes `|` but does not escape backslashes first. Markdown table cells need backslashes escaped before pipes; otherwise a literal backslash before a pipe becomes a literal backslash and leaves the pipe as a cell delimiter. Given a gate reason containing `failed \| see log`, `_cell` returns `failed \\| see log`. When rendered into a GFM table row, the two backslashes are consumed as an escaped backslash, so the following pipe is unescaped and splits the row, reintroducing the previous row-splitting failure for notes that already contain escaped pipes.

chunk_findings.detail:
The test appends a gate note `bad | see log\nnext line` and then asserts `"next line" not in text`. A correct markdown-table renderer can prevent row splitting while preserving the note, for example by rendering the cell as `bad \| see log next line` or `bad \| see log
next line`; both keep the gate outcome on one row, but both still contain the substring `next line`, so the test would reject valid output. If the test passes as shipped, it means the renderer is dropping the post-newline evidence (or the whole `standards` row), which loses red-green evidence the PR body is supposed to show. The assertion should verify that the `standards` row remains one three-cell row with escaped content, not that the note fragment disappears.

chunk_findings.detail: The pipe/newline regression locks in dropped evidence. `test_a_pipe_or_newline_in_a_gate_cell_does_not_split_its_row` records reason `bad | see log\nnext line` and then requires `"next line" not in text`. A renderer that keeps the note on one row (newline folded to a space, or escaped) fails this test; only a body that deletes everything after the newline passes. Given that note, the standards row can show `bad | see log` and still satisfy the assertion while the rest of the review reason is gone, so the gate outcome is no longer accompanied by the evidence that justified it.

chunk_findings.detail: `_cell` now Markdown-escapes backslashes before the rendered body is passed to `redact_secrets`. Given a gate note whose reason is a configured secret containing a backslash, e.g. `a\b`, and `pr_body_cell_max` large enough that the cell is not truncated, `_cell` emits `a\\b`. The PR body is then redacted as escaped Markdown; if `redact_secrets(text, cfg)` replaces configured secret values/patterns by their raw text, it will not match `a\b`, so the outward request description still contains the secret material (with extra escaping). The new escaping therefore can defeat the required secret redaction; redaction should be applied to raw derived values before Markdown escaping/truncation, or the redactor must be escaping-aware.

chunk_findings.detail: `_cell` bounds and escapes the gate note before `render_pr` runs `redact_secrets` on the finished body. A secret that would have matched in the full reason is no longer the same string once the cut lands inside it, so the redactor misses it and a prefix is published. Given `pr_body_cell_max = 24` and a gate reason `failed auth token= [REDACTED] the note cell becomes `failed auth token= [REDACTED] (the `\|`/`\\` pass is a no-op here). A GitHub-token pattern that requires `ghp_` plus 36 alphanumerics does not match, and that truncated token is what the pull-request body emits.

chunk_findings.detail: `_cell` scrubs the raw text before whitespace folding, so a configured secret that contains a space can still be created by the subsequent `split()`/join and then be truncated before the final redactor sees it. For example, with a configured literal secret `token value 1234567890`, `pr_body_cell_max` small enough to truncate (e.g. `12` if the ellipsis is one character), and a gate reason `token\nvalue 1234567890`, the call `scrub(str(text or ""))` does not match the secret because the raw text has a newline where the secret has a space. The following `split()` folds it to `token value 1234567890`; the cell is then cut to `token value…`, and the final `redact_secrets(text, cfg)` no longer matches the full secret. The outward PR body therefore prints a prefix of the configured secret, despite the change’s claim that raw redaction prevents a cut from hiding one.

chunk_findings.detail: The added second `scrub` is still applied before the Markdown-cell escaping, but escaping can itself create a configured secret. For example, if the configured literal secret is the character sequence backslash, pipe, `1`, `2`, `3` (`\|123`), the cell text is `|123`, and `cell_max=3`, both `scrub` calls see only `|123` and do not redact it; the subsequent backslash/pipe escaping turns that into `\|123`, and the truncation to `cell_max - 1` leaves `\|` (plus the ellipsis) in the cell. That is a prefix of the configured secret, and the later body redactor cannot match the full secret because it has already been cut. The new test only covers whitespace folding, not escaping-created secrets, so the redaction requirement is still violated [r-consent-outward].

chunk_findings.detail: The new `scrub` after escaping can remove the escaping backslashes themselves. If the configured literal secret is a single backslash, an input cell text such as `a|b` is escaped to `a\|b`; the added `scrub` then replaces that backslash with `[REDACTED]`, yielding `a[REDACTED]|b`. The pipe is no longer escaped, so when the value is placed in a Markdown table row it terminates the cell and can inject additional cells, even though `_cell` is supposed to return an escaped cell.

chunk_findings.detail: The added `_BARE_PIPE` pass only escapes a pipe when it has no immediately preceding backslash, but Markdown table escaping depends on the parity of the preceding backslash run. A scrub that removes an odd number of backslashes from an escaped run can leave an even positive run before the pipe; the lookbehind still sees a backslash and does nothing, so the pipe remains a live cell delimiter. For example, configure a literal secret consisting of three backslash characters and render a cell whose raw text is two backslashes followed by a pipe. The escaping step turns that into five backslashes before the pipe; the scrub replaces the first three with `[REDACTED]`, leaving two backslashes before the pipe. `_BARE_PIPE` does not replace the pipe because it is preceded by a backslash, but in Markdown the first of those two backslashes escapes the second, leaving the pipe unescaped and terminating the table cell. This is the same injection class the new line was added to prevent.
